# Nesting

- No bird gives birth to live young
- Birds prepare nests to **incubate** and **cradle** young, **control microclimate**, and **protect from predators**
- Caring for eggs and young is energetically costly! 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/nests.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (MacFarland et al. 2004; Thomson 1910)

- Open cup nests in trees with basal support are most common

# Passerine nest evolution

- Domed nests ancestral to passerines
- Open cup nests evolved multiple times in oscines and suboscines

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/nest_evol.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Price & Griffiths 2017)

# Adaptive radiation of nest architecture

- Ancestral Furnariidae (overnbird) cavity nests gave rise to diverse domed nests from vegetation and mud 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/furnariid.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Zyskowski & Prum 1999)

# Nesting is challenging

- Selection from nest loss due to **predation**, starvation, desertion, hatching failure, adverse weather

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/virginia_mt.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Lockyer et al. 2013)

# Global patterns of nest predation

- Highest nest predation rates in the tropics (figure below from songbirds)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/predation.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Matysioková & Remeš 2022)

# Climate change is flipping nest predation gradients

- Highest nest predation rates now in the Arctic for shorebirds
- Causes: declining lemming populations, behavioral shifts in foxes, vegetation changes...

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/predation2.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Kubelka et al. 2018)  

# Nest protection by predators

- Black-chinned hummingbirds nest near *Accipter* spp. nests, where Mexican Jays forage higher to avoid predation, finding fewer hummingbird eggs (example of a **trophic cascade**)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.7\linewidth]{images/trophic.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Greeney et al. 2015)

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/ghalambor.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Martin & Ghalambor 1999)

\normalsize

a) frequently feeding a partner draws predator attention
b) hole nesters are less vulnerable to predation
c) predation is more common in Arizona
d) all of the above

# Nests can protect against infection

- Generalist hummingbird Green-backed Firecrown uses a rare moss to build its nest. 
- Laboratory assays show it has better anti-microbial propertises (measured by **halo size** on plates than more common species and controls). 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/moss.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Fontúrbel et al. 2020)

# Nest microclimates impact metabolism

- Mean metabolic rates of birds perched outside nests are higher than those incubating within insulated nests

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/incubation.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Walsberg & King 1978)

# Cavity nesting drives competition

- **Primary cavity nesters** create cavities, while **secondary cavity nesters** use abandoned ones

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/cavity.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Martin et al. 2004)

# Incubation

- Eggs must be kept ~37-38°C; bad if <35°C or > 40.5°C
- Lasts anywhere from 10-80 days
- Eggs must be turned and repositioned to balance growth
- Most birds delay incubation until clutch is complete for synchronous hatching 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.6\linewidth]{images/incubate.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (DuRant et al. 2013)  

# Brood Patches

- **Brood patches** are patches of featherless skin on the underside of birds that form during nesting season
- Effectively transfers heat to incubate eggs
- Develops on the incubating sex (or sexes); under hormonal control 

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.8\linewidth]{images/brood_patch.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Deeming & Du Freu 2008)    

# Megapodes and environmental incubation

- Megapodes (Galliformes: Megapodiidae) use environmental heat sources to incubate eggs: decomposing leaf litter, geothermal activity, hot sand
- Megapode young are extremely precocial

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = 0.5\linewidth]{images/megapode.png}
\end{figure}  

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eIXOF6aSZrs&t=94s

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019; *Megapodius reinwardt*, *Alectura lathami*)

# Embryonic Development

- Developmental stages are the same across species, but time spent in each stage can differ
- Incubation periods correlated with adult longevity, precocial young, reduced predation risk

\begin{figure}
\includegraphics[width = \linewidth]{images/development.png}
\end{figure}  

\hfill \tiny (Gill et al. 2019)
